narrative:
The model determined that you have a 76% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is quite high, the law school decided to reject your application.

Three pieces of information about you drove this outcome, ranked from most to least influential. First, your class ranking at the end of your third year was very low—you placed in the bottom decile, while accepted students averaged around the middle of their class. This strongly pushed the model toward predicting failure. Second, your LSAT score of 25 sits well below the average of 37 among accepted applicants, giving the model another clear reason to expect you would struggle with the bar exam. Third, your family’s lower-middle income actually worked slightly in your favor compared with most accepted students, who more often come from upper-middle or middle-income backgrounds. However, this single positive signal was not nearly enough to offset the other two factors.

Taken together, your low academic standing in law school and modest LSAT performance outweighed everything else, leading the system to conclude the risk of failure was too great for admission.

What you should do next is focus on improving the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retake the LSAT and aim for a substantially higher score, while also working to raise your class rank in the remaining years. These concrete steps would most directly lower your predicted risk and strengthen future applications.
